I am 50 years old, and I have worked this land for 30 years. I never went to school, but I know every corner of my 3.5 mu. I watch what my neighbors do, and I do what works. My son works in Shijiazhuang and sends some money home, but fertilizer is expensive now, so I have to count every yuan. Still, I would rather put a bit more fertilizer than lose the crop — a bad harvest means my family goes hungry, but wasting a little fertilizer is just money lost.

For wheat: I always plant wheat in October. I rotary till the field first, then sow. I buy the same improved seed from the market that Old Wang across the road uses — about 30 jin per mu. At sowing, I spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu. When the wheat turns green in spring, I topdress with half a bag of urea, and at jointing I put another half bag. That is what I did last year and the year before. I irrigate three times: once before winter so the seedlings don't freeze, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. The well water costs electricity, but three times is enough. I spray herbicide once after sowing, and if I see aphids in spring, I spray once more. I expect about 1000 jin per mu if the weather is decent.

For maize: After wheat harvest in early June, I don't plough — there is no time, and everyone now plants no-till with the machine directly into the wheat stubble. I buy new hybrid maize seed every year, two and a half jin per mu. At planting I put compound fertilizer in the row, about 80 jin per mu. When the plants reach knee height, I side-dress with urea, about 30 jin per mu. I irrigate twice: once when the tassels come out, and once when the grain is filling. If it rains well, maybe only once, but I have the well if I need it. I spray herbicide once, and once for corn borer if I see holes in the leaves. I hope for 1200 jin per mu.

I don't change what works. My neighbor Li cut his fertilizer last year and his wheat was thin — I will not make that mistake. My daughter-in-law helps with spraying, and I do the rest myself. We manage.
